newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai economic woes bring calls for Amnuay to go.
newsitem.headline: Thai economic woes bring calls for Amnuay to go.

text.p: Thailand's deteriorating economy has put Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan in the spotlight, but analysts said on Monday that any suggestion he should be replaced was politically motivated without broad public support.

Some politicians in and outside the government have recently called on Amnuay, a former banker turned politician before his appointment to the finance portfolio last November, to help reverse the economic slide by stepping down.

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh scotched speculation on Sunday by ruling out any impending changes in his economic team. Chavalit did, however, pledge an increased role in working with Amnuay to manage the economy.

"Amnuay is experienced for the job, but any man in his shoes would have a tough time considering the state of the economy that we are in," said Chatchai Saelee of Chao Phaya Finance and Securities Co Ltd.

The Thai economy is in its worst shape in a decade, buffeted by weak exports, a crippled property sector, a prolonged stock market slide and embattled banks and finance firms struggling to cope with a mounting burden of non-performing loans.

Private economists forecast gross domestic product (GDP) will expand about five percent this year, against 6.7 percent in 1996 and 8.6 percent in 1995. The central bank says it expects the economy to grow at least six percent in 1997.
Analysts said recent criticism of Amnuay came partly from members of Chavalit's major coalition partner, the 52-seat Chart Pattana Party, which has quietly sought a greater say in economic policy.
They said Amnuay had been a natural victim of a deepening economic slowdown, even though the soft-spoken economist had not taken any wrong steps in his efforts to shore up the economy.

One of Amnuay's initiatives that won plaudits was a $4.1 billion cut in government and state enterprise budgets this year. The cuts were aimed at curbing the current account deficit and balancing the national budget.
The Thai government, facing a sharp fall in tax revenue, is heading for its first budget deficit in 10 years this year.

"(Amnuay) has not stumbled or made any mistakes but his record could also not be described as outstanding either. His performance has not been that impressive," said one analyst at a finance firm who declined to be identified.

But Chatchai of Chao Phaya Finance and Securities echoed other analysts and said replacing Amnuay would do more harm than good for business confidence. He said Chavalit's coalition partners would find it hard to find a successor who could match Amnuay's highly respected background.

Former Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda was probably the only banker favoured by the market as a good replacement for Amnuay, analysts said. Tarrin is an elected member of parliament representing the opposition Democrat Party.
Thira Ashakul of the Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand said Amnuay could not be faulted for mistakes but lacked an aggressive management style, especially in boosting sluggish exports.

Thai exports contracted 0.2 percent in 1996 after growing more than 20 percent a year for most of the decade. Exports rose a disappointing one percent during the first four months of 1997 against seven percent growth a year ago.

Thira said, however, that Amnuay could be seen as tainted by being part of a government that had failed to show political will in tackling economic problems, including delays in privatising state enterprises and implementing infrastructure projects.
